  "title": "Commitment Depth Routing: Selective Video Activation in Video-Action Models",
  "core_problem": "Video-Action Models (VAMs) like mimic-video train their action decoder robust to any τ_v ∈ [0,1] via logit-normal sampling, making τ_v a flexible test-time parameter. A foundational finding from mimic-video (arXiv:2512.15692): τ_v=1 (pure noise video input, single backbone forward pass) achieves 46.9% task success on SIMPLER-Bridge and is described as 'a good default value that balances policy performance and inference speed' — the compute-efficient recommended starting point. Critically, Figure 5 of mimic-video shows aggregate performance peaks at an intermediate noise level (not at τ_v=1), and Table I does not enumerate a fixed-global-τ_v sweep — meaning a fixed τ_v=0.8 or τ_v=0.7 applied uniformly may outperform τ_v=1 on performance alone at the cost of more compute. τ_v=0 (fully denoised video) gives WORSE autonomous policy performance than intermediate τ_v values — confirmed by mimic-video — so the action-quality-optimal range excludes both extremes. The per-task τ_v sweep yields +9.4pp on SIMPLER-Bridge (46.9%→56.3%), proving SOME tasks genuinely benefit from actual video denoising (τ_v < 1). Fast-WAM (arXiv:2603.16666) achieves 97.6% LIBERO by skipping test-time future video generation entirely, confirming the high-τ_v regime is strong on average. The core gap is a selective video activation problem: which observations within which tasks need video denoising below τ_v=1 (or below whatever fixed intermediate value would be globally best), and can this be predicted zero-shot without expensive per-task offline rollouts?

Existing approaches are non-adaptive: (1) LingBot-VA (RSS 2026) fixes τ_v≈0.6 uniformly — imposes video denoising costs even where τ_v=1 suffices and may misallocate compute away from phases where a different threshold is optimal; (2) Fast-WAM skips video entirely via architectural retraining — effective on average but permanently loses gains for tasks where video is genuinely critical; (3) mimic-video's per-task sweeping requires ~10 rollouts per new task at deployment time. No system selectively activates video denoising only for observations where it materially improves action quality relative to the compute-efficient τ_v=1 default, and no paper has empirically studied which manipulation phases within 3D episodes benefit from τ_v < 1. CDR addresses this: default to τ_v=1 (compute-efficient, strong baseline), activate video denoising (route to τ_v < 1) only when predicted necessary, and Pareto-dominate both uniform-denoising approaches (LingBot-VA-style) and the τ_v=1 fixed baseline on the task-success vs. mean-τ_v-consumed frontier.",
  "opportunity": "The key enabling property is mimic-video's variable-τ_v training (logit-normal over [0,1]), which makes the action decoder capable of exploiting richer video features at lower τ_v while remaining functional at τ_v=1. CDR exploits this asymmetry: a lightweight router that defaults to τ_v=1 — compute-efficient and recommended by mimic-video — and activates actual video denoising (routes to τ_v < 1) only for observations where the action decoder's output demonstrably benefits from real video structure, as measured by proximity to ground-truth demonstration actions.

The key insight from mimic-video Figure 5 is that aggregate performance peaks at intermediate τ_v values (not at τ_v=1), yet τ_v=1 is recommended as the default because it requires only a single backbone forward pass. This means: (a) uniform intermediate τ_v (LingBot-VA's approach) may outperform τ_v=1 on performance but wastes compute on frames that don't need it; (b) CDR can Pareto-dominate uniform intermediate τ_v by selectively applying lower τ_v only to frames where quality gains are empirically justified. CDR asks: 'which frames are exceptions to the τ_v=1 efficiency default, and can we learn to identify them zero-shot?' The per-task sweep gain (+9.4pp) proves exceptions exist at task scale; CDR's Phase 1 study asks whether they cluster in specific manipulation phases (grasp, insert) within tasks.

Two publishable outcomes with asymmetric CoRL value: (1) If per-observation τ_v* < 1 frames concentrate in precision phases with >2pp per-phase improvement: CDR demonstrates selective video activation as a Pareto-superior alternative to both Fast-WAM (universal skip) and LingBot-VA (universal partial denoising) — the router outperforms both fixed baselines on the task-success vs. mean-τ_v-consumed Pareto frontier, on SIMPLER-Bridge. (2) If within-task per-phase variation is small (<2pp): task-level CDR router recovers ≥80% of per-task sweep gain (+7.5pp of +9.4pp) zero-shot on SIMPLER-Bridge — a concrete deployment contribution automating mimic-video's expensive per-task offline sweep via a frozen MLP trained on LIBERO-100 task embeddings. Outcome 2 must be framed with specific numerical targets (≥80% recovery) to meet CoRL bar; 'validation study alone' is insufficient.",
  "landscape": "LingBot-VA (arXiv:2601.21998, RSS 2026, Ant Group) is CDR's primary comparison. Noisy History Augmentation (saug ∈ [0.5,1.0] during training) enables fixed 3-step inference to s=0.6. Key distinction from CDR: LingBot-VA imposes a LOWER τ_v (more denoising) than the compute-efficient τ_v=1 default uniformly across all frames, assuming this universally improves performance. CDR's critical empirical test: is uniform τ_v=0.6 better or worse than selective activation (default τ_v=1, activate only when predicted necessary) on the Pareto frontier of task success vs. mean τ_v consumed? If CDR matches LingBot-VA's performance at lower mean τ_v, or exceeds LingBot-VA on precision tasks where the optimal activation threshold differs from 0.6, CDR demonstrates a Pareto-superior operating point. 98.5% LIBERO (Spatial 98.5, Object 99.6, Goal 97.2, Long 98.5), 92.2% RoboTwin. No per-phase analysis; fixed threshold assumed without verification.

mimic-video (arXiv:2512.15692, Dec 2025) is CDR's base model. Key findings: (a) τ_v=1 is described as 'a good default value that balances policy performance and inference speed,' achieving 46.9% scratch SIMPLER-Bridge — the compute-efficient recommended default; (b) Figure 5 shows aggregate performance peaks at an intermediate noise level (not at τ_v=1), meaning selective intermediate routing can outperform the τ_v=1 baseline on quality while CDR keeps mean compute low; (c) per-task sweep yields +9.4pp (46.9%→56.3%); (d) τ_v=0 gives WORSE performance than intermediate τ_v — the sweep range excludes τ_v=0. Note: mimic-video Table I does NOT enumerate fixed-global-τ_v comparisons (τ_v=0.5 vs 0.7 vs 0.9 vs 1.0) — CDR's Phase 3 baselines will be the first such systematic comparison on SIMPLER-Bridge. 93.9% LIBERO, 46.9%/56.3% SIMPLER-Bridge.

Fast-WAM (arXiv:2603.16666, Mar 2026) removes test-time future video prediction by processing only the first clean observation frame — architecturally different from τ_v=1 (which passes noisy future frames through the full backbone). 97.6% LIBERO, 91.8% RoboTwin, 4× speedup; requires retraining. Important: Fast-WAM does NOT evaluate on SIMPLER-Bridge (results reported only on LIBERO and RoboTwin) — there is no Fast-WAM SIMPLER-Bridge number to compare against. CDR is post-hoc (no backbone retraining) and occupies the selective middle: defer to Fast-WAM-style efficiency (τ_v=1) by default, activate actual video generation for precision-critical frames. On SIMPLER-Bridge, CDR's baseline (a) τ_v=1 serves as the closest achievable proxy for Fast-WAM's test-time behavior on the mimic-video backbone.

VADF: Vision-Adaptive Diffusion Policy Framework (arXiv:2604.15938, Apr 2026) adapts ACTION diffusion denoising steps per task stage via a Hierarchical Vision Task Segmenter — orthogonal to CDR. VADF modifies the action diffusion process (fewer steps for simple actions, more for complex); CDR modifies the VIDEO backbone denoising depth (τ_v). These address different computational bottlenecks and can be combined. VADF is evaluated on simpler manipulation setups (Push-T, Adroit, ARX5); CDR targets WAM-class models on SIMPLER-Bridge and LIBERO-100.

DiT4DiT (arXiv:2603.10448) ablation: single-step (high τ_v) is best on average — independently confirms the high-τ_v regime is a strong global default, supporting CDR's corrected framing. 98.6% LIBERO, 50.8% RoboCasa. DreamZero (arXiv:2602.15922, Feb 2026, 14B WAM) caches velocity within a denoising trajectory; complementary to CDR (reduces cost within given τ_v level vs. CDR choosing the τ_v level). ChEaP (arXiv:2603.30043) establishes early plan commitment in 2D mazes (first few denoising steps commit high-level motion; further steps add visual detail only); CDR empirically validates and extends this to 3D manipulation video backbones.

Denoising, Fast and Slow (CVPR 2026, arXiv:2604.19141) introduces the Patch Forcing (PF) Framework for per-PATCH spatial difficulty routing within images: easier image regions complete denoising earlier while harder regions receive more denoising steps — computation varies spatially WITHIN a single generated image. DIFFERENTIATION from CDR: CDR operates in the temporal domain (routing across trajectory timesteps — which frames in a manipulation episode need video backbone denoising), while Denoising Fast and Slow operates in the spatial domain (which patches within a single frame need more steps). These are orthogonal axes that could in principle be combined (spatial patch routing within each CDR-selected frame). Note: this paper is about image generation, not robot action models, and is cited as feasibility motivation only.

MotuBrain (arXiv:2604.27792) is a unified VAM with Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture under a UniDiffuser formulation, supporting policy learning, world modeling, video generation, and inverse dynamics. Achieves 95.8%+ on RoboTwin 2.0 under clean and randomized settings with 50× speedup via step reduction, compilation, and FP8 quantization. DIFFERENTIATION from CDR: MotuBrain is a training-time architectural approach for unified multimodal modeling; CDR is post-hoc test-time routing on a frozen mimic-video checkpoint requiring no backbone retraining. These are complementary — MotuBrain could serve as a future CDR base model if it supports variable-τ_v inference. Reviewers may mention MotuBrain as related work; distinguish on training-time architecture vs. test-time routing.

D3P (arXiv:2508.06804) adapts ACTION denoising steps via RL — complementary efficiency axis (same as VADF, different mechanism). X-WAM (arXiv:2604.26694) uses Asynchronous Noise Sampling from a fixed joint distribution — not per-observation adaptive. UWM (arXiv:2504.02792) uses independent modality timesteps from fixed schedule. Being-H0.7 (arXiv:2605.00078) avoids pixel decoding via distillation. S-VAM (arXiv:2603.16195) distills multi-step to one-step; requires retraining. 'When to Trust Imagination' (arXiv:2605.06222) reduces replanning frequency; orthogonal to per-call CDR.

No existing VAM paper: (a) uses GT-action-referenced τ_v labeling; (b) studies which 3D manipulation phases need τ_v < 1 empirically; or (c) trains a zero-shot per-task/per-observation τ_v predictor that generalizes across tasks without offline rollouts.",
  "approach": "CDR has four sequenced phases relative to a deployed mimic-video checkpoint (no backbone retraining required):

**Phase 0 — Sanity Check (1–2 H100-hours, PREREQUISITE, run immediately):**
Take 5 LIBERO tasks spanning types (2 precision grasp/insert, 2 pick-and-place, 1 long-horizon). Run 3 demonstration trajectories each (~1,500 frames total). Sweep τ_v ∈ {1.0, 0.9, ..., 0.1} using the frozen mimic-video action decoder. Compute τ_v*(f) = argmin_{τ_v ∈ {1.0,...,0.1}} ||a_{τ_v}(f) − a_GT(f)||₂ for each frame f (GT action from demo teleop). Annotate frames by manipulation phase using end-effector distance to target + gripper state.

Decision gate (by May 12):
- If <10% of frames have τ_v* < 0.9 (nearly all frames prefer τ_v=1 for action quality): per-observation variation is minimal. Pivot paper framing to 'τ_v=1 universality study + automated zero-shot per-task routing' — do NOT commit to full Phase 1 scope. Reframe contribution as empirical validation + deployment automation.
- If ≥20% of frames have τ_v* < 0.9 AND these cluster in grasp/insert phases: full CDR selective activation story is empirically supported. Proceed to Phase 1.
- Intermediate (10–20%): assess within-episode vs. across-task variance before proceeding.

**Phase 1 — 3D Video Necessity Study (~40–60 H100-hours):**
For each frame f in LIBERO-100 (100 tasks × 50 demos × ~100 steps ≈ 500K frames), compute:

  τ_v*(f) = argmin_{τ_v ∈ {1.0, 0.9, ..., 0.1}} ||a_{τ_v}(f) − a_GT(f)||₂

where a_GT(f) is the ground-truth demonstration action at frame f (available from LIBERO-100 teleop data) and a_{τ_v}(f) is the mimic-video action decoder output with τ_v-noised video input. The sweep range {1.0,...,0.1} excludes τ_v=0 entirely (confirmed worse than intermediate τ_v in mimic-video).

Annotate frames with manipulation phases: approach (end-effector distance > 5cm to target), pre-grasp (distance 1–5cm, gripper open), grasp (gripper closing event), transport (gripper closed, object moving), place (object near target, gripper opening). Derive from proprioceptive state; no additional network required.

Report: (a) Distribution of τ_v* — specifically fraction of frames where τ_v*=1.0 (no activation needed) vs. τ_v* < 0.9; (b) Mean τ_v* by manipulation phase — do grasp/insert phases have significantly lower τ_v* than approach/transport? (c) Within-episode τ_v* variance vs. across-task τ_v* variance — which dominates? (d) Whether LingBot-VA's fixed s≈0.6 corresponds to over-denoising for approach frames and potentially misaligned thresholds for other phases.

[Distribution shift mitigation]: Include suboptimal rollout states to reduce demo-vs-rollout gap. Specifically: run the mimic-video policy (τ_v=1) 3× per task on LIBERO-100, collect frames from failed/recovery trajectories (partial grasps, dropped objects, recovery approaches). Add these to the labeling dataset (~50% of total labeled frames from non-expert trajectories). This gives the router diverse training states including recovery behaviors seen during closed-loop evaluation.

Compute: ~750K frames × 10 τ_v levels = ~7.5M backbone forward passes. With batch=64 on Cosmos-Predict2 (2B DiT), ~40–60 H100-hours.

**Phase 2 — Router Training (~5 H100-hours):**
4-class router: {τ_v=1.0 (no activation), τ_v∈[0.7,0.9] (light activation), τ_v∈[0.4,0.6] (medium activation), τ_v∈[0.1,0.3] (heavy activation)}. Labels from Phase 1 mapped to nearest class bin. Architecture: two-layer MLP (512-dim CLIP image embedding + 512-dim frozen mimic-video language embedding → 256-dim hidden ReLU → 4-class softmax). Loss: CE(τ̂, τ_v*_class) + λ·E[τ̂_consumed].

Conservative routing (addressing distribution shift): if max softmax probability < θ, predict τ_v=1.0 regardless of argmax — since τ_v=1 is the compute-efficient default, falling back to it on uncertain (OOD) states avoids unnecessary compute overhead. Sweep λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 0.5} and θ ∈ {0.5, 0.7, 0.9} to trace the accuracy-efficiency frontier.

Task-level CDR variant: also train on task-mean τ_v* (average τ_v* across all frames in a task) to enable the per-task routing baseline (d) and test zero-shot generalization on SIMPLER-Bridge.

**Phase 3 — Evaluation (~50 H100-hours, primary benchmark: SIMPLER-Bridge):**

Baselines:
(a) mimic-video τ_v=1 global (compute-efficient recommended default per mimic-video paper, 46.9% SIMPLER, 93.9% LIBERO). NOTE: this baseline also serves as CDR's closest achievable proxy for Fast-WAM's test-time video-skipping behavior on the mimic-video backbone — Fast-WAM (arXiv:2603.16666) does not evaluate on SIMPLER-Bridge and requires architectural retraining, so direct comparison is impossible; the narrative in the paper notes this distinction explicitly rather than claiming to replicate Fast-WAM.
(b) LingBot-VA-style fixed τ_v=0.5 on mimic-video base (primary CDR comparison — tests whether uniform partial denoising beats selective activation)
(c) LingBot-VA-style fixed τ_v=0.7 and τ_v=0.9 (systematic fixed-threshold sweep; NOTE: this is ALSO the first published fixed-global-τ_v comparison on SIMPLER-Bridge — mimic-video Table I does not include this sweep. Results will empirically determine whether a fixed intermediate τ_v outperforms τ_v=1 globally, and set the fixed-threshold Pareto frontier for fair CDR comparison)
(d) Per-task CDR router (predict task-mean τ_v* zero-shot on SIMPLER-Bridge — primary fallback result; claim: recovers ≥80% of +9.4pp sweep gain = ≥7.5pp without offline rollouts)
(e) Per-observation CDR (full system)
(f) Per-task sweep oracle (56.3% SIMPLER — upper bound)

Primary results: Pareto curves (task success vs. mean τ_v consumed) on SIMPLER-Bridge. LIBERO-100 results reported secondarily for comparability. Key empirical claims:
1. Per-observation CDR Pareto-dominates all fixed-threshold baselines (a,b,c) on SIMPLER-Bridge — matching or exceeding the best fixed intermediate τ_v at strictly lower mean compute, OR at higher task success with the same mean compute budget
2. Per-task CDR recovers ≥80% of per-task sweep gain zero-shot on SIMPLER-Bridge
3. CDR allocates lower τ_v (more video activation) to grasp-phase frames than approach frames — interpretability via per-phase τ_v heatmaps

Ablations: per-phase τ_v allocation analysis (grasp vs. approach); precision task subset (peg insertion, mug hanging) vs. coarse tasks; conservative routing ablation (θ sweep); zero-shot generalization from LIBERO-100 router to SIMPLER-Bridge tasks (no retraining — key deployment story).

Note on absolute LIBERO numbers: CDR built on mimic-video (93.9%) will fall below LingBot-VA (98.5%) and DiT4DiT (98.6%) due to base model gap. Paper leads with SIMPLER-Bridge Pareto curves in abstract/intro, framed as: 'SIMPLER-Bridge is a real-to-sim transfer benchmark where most methods score under 55%; 46.9% represents state-of-the-art for models of this parameter class, and CDR's gain is measured against this competitive baseline.' LIBERO results in supplementary for comparability. Framing is explicit in introduction: 'Our contribution is the selective activation principle and zero-shot deployment, not absolute SOTA on LIBERO.'

**Timeline for CoRL 2026 (May 29 deadline):**
- Phase 0: run May 10–11 (1–2 H100-hours, 1–2 days)
- Phase 0 gate decision: May 12
- Phase 1 (if positive): May 12–18 (40–60h, with 8 H100s = 5–8 days)
- Phase 2: May 18–19 (~1 day)
- Phase 3: May 19–25 (50h / 8 H100s = ~6 days; RoboCasa and per-phase heatmap ablations are explicitly drop-able if Phase 1 runs long — minimum viable submission requires only SIMPLER-Bridge primary Pareto curves plus per-task CDR zero-shot result)
- Write-up: May 25–28 (4 days; if Phase 1 takes 8 days, writing compresses to 2 days — acceptable for a focused Pareto-curve paper)
- Buffer: May 29 submission

## SimplerEnv and SIMPLER Overview

SIMPLER is a suite of open-source simulated evaluation environments for common real robot manipulation setups, namely the Google Robot evaluations from the RT-series of works, and environments from the BridgeData V2 dataset.

**Robot Embodiments:**
SIMPLER can be used to evaluate diverse sets of rigid-body tasks for each of two robot embodiments: Google Robot and WidowX.

**BridgeData Integration:**
SIMPLER includes simulated evaluation environments for the Google Robot from the RT series of works and the WidowX BridgeV2 setup.

## Evaluation Methodologies

SIMPLER encompasses two distinct evaluation approaches:

Visual Matching evaluation: Matching real & sim visual appearances for policy evaluation by overlaying real-world images onto simulation backgrounds and adjusting foreground object and robot textures in simulation.

Variant Aggregation evaluation: creating different sim environment variants (e.g., different backgrounds, lightings, distractors, table textures, etc) and averaging their results.
